subject: Archaeology
title: The Tiara of Saitaphernes
description: One-minute skill: The Tiara of Saitaphernes.

hook.text: The Louvre bought a golden tiara in 1896 for 200,000 francs, calling it a masterpiece of ancient Greek goldwork.

buildup.text: The tiara depicted scenes from Homer's Iliad in exquisite detail.

discovery.text: A Russian goldsmith named Israel Rouchomovsky came forward in 1903 and said he had made it.

twist.text: The Louvre had ignored warnings from scholars who spotted anachronistic details.

climax.text: The scandal embarrassed France's greatest museum and led to stricter authentication procedures worldwide.

punchline.text: The Louvre paid a fortune for a tiara made by a living craftsman.

quiz.question: How was the Tiara of Saitaphernes exposed as a forgery?
options: Chemical analysis proved the gold was mined in modern Russia
The Russian goldsmith who made it came forward and demonstrated his technique
X-rays revealed a hidden message inside the metalwork

details.summary: In 1896 the Louvre purchased a golden tiara supposedly from a Scythian king for 200,000 francs. It was actually made by a modern goldsmith in Odessa named Israel Rouchomovsky, who eventually came forward and demonstrated his craftsmanship to prove the museum had been duped.
details.whyItMatters: The tiara scandal embarrassed one of the world's greatest museums and demonstrated that even expert curators can be deceived when desire for a spectacular acquisition overrides careful authentication.
takeaways: The Louvre bought a forged golden Scythian tiara in 1896
Goldsmith Israel Rouchomovsky eventually proved he made it
The scandal showed that desire for prestige overrode caution

faq.question: How was the forgery eventually exposed?
faq.answer: After years of scholarly doubt, Rouchomovsky traveled to Paris and demonstrated his goldsmithing techniques, recreating details from the tiara. His proven skill and knowledge of the piece's construction left no doubt. The Louvre quietly removed the tiara from display.

faq.question: Why did the Louvre fall for the forgery?
faq.answer: Competition between European museums for spectacular acquisitions created pressure to buy quickly. The tiara's artistry was genuinely superb, and experts interpreted its features through their desire for it to be authentic rather than critically examining inconsistencies.
